slidetranscripts.slidetranscript:
Welcome to “Content Knowledge,” the second session of the Reading Street 2013 Product Implementation Essentials Self-Paced Course. This session should take you approximately 75 minutes to complete.

You’ll need your Participant Workbook and your Teacher’s Edition for this session. Go ahead and get these resources. When you’re ready to move on, click Next.

Before we begin, let’s review what we learned in Session 1.

We examined four focus areas of the Common Core State Standards that are incorporated into Reading Street 2013 instruction: Content Knowledge, Text-Based Comprehension, Writing, and Foundational Skills.

We explored the unit and weekly lesson structure, and examined unit-level planning resources like the Skills Overview page.

We also reviewed weekly planning pages such as Preview Your Week and 5-Day Planner.

We also took a look at two additional resources-the Assessment and Assessment Checkpoints for the Week pages-that illustrate how assessment is incorporated into the program.

You also watched a video that highlighted how four Reading Street educators plan for instruction and had an opportunity to begin developing a weekly planning organizer.


If you want to review the entire session, you can access Session 2 on the online platform.

Now, let’s look at the Session 2 objectives.

By the end of this session you will be able to:
-Implement Reading Street lesson features that develop students’ content knowledge.

-Create a concept board to aid in students’ transfer of knowledge.

Let’s look back to the Preview Your Week page in your Teacher’s Edition, which we examined during Session 1. This page provides a starting point for thinking about the role that content knowledge plays in Reading Street instruction and the specific program features and resources you’ll use to address it.

Click the play button to watch a video clip that summarizes the information included on the Preview Your Week page.

When you’re ready to move on, click Next.

According to the Common Core State Standards, texts should be arranged so that students develop content knowledge in other content areas. This page outlines the knowledge students can gain during a week of instruction using a variety of resources. Weekly Science and Social Studies Knowledge Goals integrate knowledge and ideas as students access multiple texts. Students develop a concept-related graphic organizer over the course of each week as the class adds new vocabulary and concepts that they have learned. Students build oral vocabulary with each week’s Amazing Words

You’ll dig deeper into how to address content knowledge in your classroom as you move through Session 2.

Take a moment now to reflect on the Content Knowledge section of Common Core 101 that you read prior to beginning today’s session.

As you reflect on what you read, consider the following question:

What role does building content knowledge play in reading instruction?

Keep this question in mind as you move through Session 2.

Ok, let’s zoom in on content knowledge!

We learned in Session 1 that content knowledge is one of the main areas of focus for developing students who are college and career ready.

To address the focus on content knowledge, the Common Core State Standards call for an interdisciplinary approach to literacy. Students in Common Core classrooms have opportunities to apply literacy to understanding in other content areas-such as science and social studies. Reading selections are systematically arranged to promote deeper understanding, and students acquire content knowledge through a variety of reading, writing, speaking, and listening activities.

This approach helps produce students who are capable of independently reading complex informational text across various content areas.

Well, clearly in Reading Street, we're teaching comprehension skills and vocabulary and vocabulary acquisition skills with the hope that you'll use those not only in Reading Street but also in all the other reading you're doing, you know, in your science class, in your social studies class, even in your math class. And by the way, when you're reading out there on your own, not for any class, because we believe firmly that the comprehension strategies and the various activities that we're engaging kids in are transferable. They're transferable in the sense that if you can use those skills to try to unpack the really important ideas in a science or a social studies text, these are the very strategies that will enable you to ask yourself, "What do I really need to learn and remember in this text?" That's really what we're all about in Reading Street.

Now let’s take a closer look at how Reading Street 2013 addresses this focus on content knowledge.

First we’ll review two useful planning resources.

A good place to start as you begin thinking about how you’ll incorporate content knowledge into instruction is the Concept Launch page.

Pause the video and open your Teacher’s Edition to unit planning page xiv so that you can follow along with me. Click Play to continue.

Remember that each unit of Reading Street instruction is organized around a Big Idea and a Big Question. Every text students read, regardless of whether it is fiction or nonfiction, relates back to the Big Question.

For example, during a unit built around the Big Question What are some patterns in nature? Grade 4 students read a myth that explains the pattern of day and night as well as an expository text about weather patterns.

The Concept Launch page illustrates how the Big Question and the weekly questions that support it provide a context and foundation for supporting student understanding across content areas.

Click the icons for more information on how to plan your weekly instruction.

To further support content knowledge, Reading Street 2013 provides weekly content-area knowledge goals. Look to the Content Knowledge Page for a week-by-week overview of these goals.

Pause the video and turn to page xxii, the Content Knowledge Page, in your Teacher’s Edition. Click Play when you’re ready to continue.

Here you’ll see that each box lists the weekly main selection title, the weekly question, and weekly content-area knowledge goals. This tie to the content areas of social studies and science allows students to read, write, and research across the curriculum. It also helps you focus on developing the skills students need to be college and career ready.

It’s time to Pause and Reflect! Before continuing, please respond to the Session 2 Pause and Reflect question in the Participant Workbook.

When you’re ready to move on, click Next.

Now let’s look at some of the lesson features that are built into the daily Content Knowledge lesson. It’s critical that you incorporate these features into your Reading Street instruction as they support the literature, discussions, and key assignments that you’ll have students complete throughout the week.

Pause the video and turn to any Day 1 Content Knowledge lesson in your Teacher’s Edition. You’ll find this lesson immediately after the weekly planning pages-look for the green border. Click Play when you’re ready to continue.

Each week of Reading Street instruction begins with a Content Knowledge lesson. As you engage your students in Concept Talk, you’ll discuss the Question of the Week. Use this discussion to help them make connections between the selections they’re reading and the unit concept.

The discussion that you lead during Concept Talk is critical to the success of the lesson and essential for supporting students’ comprehension of the week’s texts and assignments. It also gives you an opportunity to connect reading skills with speaking and listening skills.

Look for for eStreet Interactive features-such as the Concept Talk Video-to support your instruction. Use these interactive features to help students build important media skills as they develop content knowledge.

During the Content Knowledge lesson, you’ll create a concept map that visually displays connections between reading selections and the unit concept. Refer your students to the concept map throughout the week.

The daily Content Knowledge lesson also includes a focus on building oral vocabulary. This is when you introduce and practice the weekly Amazing Words.

Use these Amazing Words to support content knowledge by extending your students’ ability to comprehend, discuss, and write about the unit and weekly concepts.
On Day 1, use the Teacher Read Aloud to introduce students to Amazing Words in the context of a reading selection. You’ll then use the Robust Vocabulary Routine to teach Amazing Words.

Throughout the week, lead your students in using Amazing Words during conversations about text, when retelling a story, in their daily writing, and during end-of-day discussions.

Monitor Progress boxes help you check in to see if students demonstrate understanding of the Amazing Words. Refer to the If…then…statements for remediation suggestions.
In the Day 5 Concept Wrap Up, help your students apply the information they have learned and use the Amazing Words to create Amazing Ideas that relate to the weekly concept. This oral vocabulary development enhances class discussions as it builds your students’ content knowledge.
To review the content covered in this Learn section, take a few moments to respond to the Session 2 Quick Check questions.

Now you’ll have a chance to see Reading Street content knowledge instruction in action!

This video illustrates how two Reading Street teachers promote content knowledge by implementing some of the Reading Street lesson features you just learned about. After watching the video, you will be asked to respond to two reflection questions in your Participant Workbook.

Once you have watched the video, respond to the following Content Knowledge video reflection questions in your Participant Workbook.

How do the teachers use the Question of the Week to develop students’ understanding of the unit concept?

Identify one Reading Street feature or resource-in addition to the Question of the Week-that the teachers use to support students’ understanding of the concept. Describe how they incorporate this resource into instruction.

When you’re ready to move on, click Next.

An effective way to illustrate content knowledge in your classroom and to support students’ transfer of knowledge between content areas is through concept boards. Let’s see how this could be done in a third-grade Reading Street classroom.

"I create a new concept board at the beginning of every unit. I start by posting the Unit Big Idea and Big Question. On Day 1 of each week, I add the weekly question along with the main selection and paired selection titles. I also post the weekly content knowledge goals. Students love helping me add content to the board throughout the week. Every day we add new Amazing Words. This is also where we add to our concept map each day."

"In my classroom the concept board serves as a reference for students as they make sense of new information-especially when we read more challenging expository texts or texts that focus on social studies or science content. It’s a constant visual reminder of the connections between all that we study in each unit."

Now you’ll have a chance to design a concept board of your own! Review the sample concept boards, and create an outline for one that you can use in your own classroom. Refer to the directions in the Participant Workbook.

When you’re ready to move on, click Next.

It’s time to share your thoughts with your peers! Go to the Discussion Board and respond to the Session 2 Discussion Board question as you reflect on the role that content knowledge plays in Reading Street instruction.

When you’re ready to move on, click Next.

Let’s review what we learned in this session.

We began by exploring two resources you’ll use to plan successful content knowledge instruction. First we looked at the Concept Launch page, which illustrates how the Big and weekly questions provide a context and foundation for supporting student understanding across content areas.

Then we saw how the Content Knowledge page provides weekly content-area knowledge goals.

Next, we looked at the daily Content Knowledge lesson and examined how you’ll use Concept Talk, a Concept Map, and Amazing Words to develop students’ content knowledge.

Then you watched a video that showcased the implementation of some of the features you’d just explored.

Finally, you heard a firsthand account about the usefulness of concept boards in supporting content knowledge and then had an opportunity to create an outline for one to be used in your own classroom.

In the next session, you’ll learn how Reading Street addresses Foundational Skills and Text-Based Comprehension. Be sure to complete the following tasks before beginning self-paced Session 3.

-Read the Text-Based Comprehension, Close Reading, and Foundational Skills sections in Common Core 101.

- Continue filling out the Navigating the Teacher’s Edition chart in your Participant Workbook for pages covered during this session.

-Continue filling out the Organizing for Instruction graphic organizer in the Participant Workbook.

-Respond to two Discussion Board posts from other participants.

Now, show what you know! Visit the course homepage to take the assessment for Session 2.

We’ll see you again in Session 3!
